why: so he faces the fear in a place that looks like it

reason: the beat is his growing recognition, not the world visibly worsening

reason: the beat is what he learns about the threat ahead, not a world getting worse

reason: the beat is the threat becoming known before it is ever seen, not the world worsening

label: State of the world deteriorates; increased awareness

label: A random ally appears; will return later

label: Community is liberated; balance is restored
why: so the reader sees the victory changed everyone, not just the hero

label: Hero and companions establish a community
why: so the quest ends in a new life built, not just a prize won

label: Hero appears whole for all the future
reason: Beat is the protagonist made permanently whole; the concept explicitly teaches the WORLD after, 'not just your protagonist' — the opposite emphasis.
why: so the change reads as permanent, not a mood that will wear off

label: Hero emerges to win the prize; role in the Kingdom
reason: Beat is the protagonist's ELEVATION (station, recognition, prize); concept teaches community-after and says nothing about making the reward specific or unholdable by the old self. Proposed: the-reward — 'The Reward (Rise in Station)'.
why: so the ending repays everything the lowly opening made us want for them

label: Hero finds fulfillment in reconnecting with humanity
why: so the redemption is proved by people letting him back in

label: Protagonist is given the elixir
why: so the later rescue was planted early and never feels like cheating

label: Protagonist in false identity; believes not worthy
why: so we see the armour before we see the wound it hides

label: Protagonist is living in a false identity
why: so the fall comes from the lie he refuses to drop

label: Protagonist is living in a false identity or anonymous
why: so we can watch the mask crack and the real self appear

label: Protagonist overwhelmed with despair; retreats to false identity
reason: Concept teaches ESTABLISHING the mask in Act 1; this is the despair-driven RELAPSE. lowest-point literally names it — 'the goal looks lost and the mask goes back on'.
why: so the mask going back on shows how much the change costs

label: Protagonist presented with admirable, desirable qualities
reason: No mask here at all — the beat makes the audience love him SO THE FALL HURTS. Bolted onto the false-identity regex to force a match (mirror of the proven rebirth-redemption defect). Proposed: admirable-first — 'Admirable First (Set Up the Fall)'.
why: so the audience loves him first and the fall actually hurts

label: Protagonist presented with unlikeable, inhumane qualities
reason: The known live defect: no mask, no pretence — he is made repellent so the later change is worth something. Proposed: unlikeable-first — 'Unlikeable First (Set Up the Redemption)'.
why: so the redemption lands — we must dislike him before he changes

label: Things out of control; retreats to false identity
reason: In tragedy this retreat is not a temporary low but a refusal to change — he clings harder to the lie as things collapse. Concept teaches Act 1 mask-building only. Proposed: doubling-down — 'Doubling Down'.
why: so his refusal to drop the lie is what destroys him

label: Protagonist's goal here is general; something normal
why: so we know their ordinary life before the story wrecks it

label: Herald gives special piece of information
why: so the news that changes everything arrives from outside, not from their head

label: Protagonist receives a warning; threat becomes visible
reason: Concept teaches WITHHOLDING the threat ('the less you show, the larger it feels') — the exact opposite of a beat where the threat becomes visible and a warning is delivered.
why: so the danger stops being rumour and the reader starts to worry

label: We become aware of the monster from a distance
why: so the monster feels huge before we ever see it

label: We gradually learn of its reputation
why: so what people say about it does the frightening for you

label: DREAM STAGE - THE SPECIAL WORLD - THE JOURNEY
reason: This is a stage BANNER, not a beat — it currently offers no examples and no chips. Either drop it from the beat rows or map it to special-world.
why: so the new world feels wondrous first and uneasy underneath

label: HIGHER STAKES
reason: Matches nothing, so no help at all on a row whose job is escalation; obstacles teaches exactly that ('each obstacle harder than the last').
why: so every failure now costs more and the reader cannot relax

label: TURNING POINT #1: Opportunity
reason: Unmatched. This is the inciting event that arrives from outside — call-to-adventure is written for it.
why: so something from outside forces the story to start

label: TURNING POINT #2: Change of Plans
reason: Unmatched. The student must write the new plan — sees-way-to-fix teaches 'a decision plus an action, too simple to work'.
why: so the protagonist now has a clear goal we can watch them chase

label: TURNING POINT #3: Point of No Return
reason: Unmatched. threshold is the point-of-no-return concept ('once across, going back is not simple').
why: so going back becomes impossible and they must see it through

label: TURNING POINT #4: Major Setback
reason: Unmatched. 'Major setback' is the all-is-lost beat lowest-point describes.
why: so everything they built collapses and the change has to be earned back

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so the collapse begins that he will never recover from

label: TURNING POINT #5: Climax
reason: Unmatched. fatal-blow is the climax concept — but note it insists the protagonist must be the one who acts, which is false in tragedy, where the decisive act is usually done TO them.
why: so the story delivers the showdown it promised, done by them

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so the promised showdown happens on the page, and he loses it

label: TURNING POINT: Anticipation
reason: Unmatched. Sits in Stage I; the job is unease before any event, which is exactly storm-coming ('atmosphere, not event').
why: so the reader feels something coming before anything actually happens

label: Protagonist in state of youthful naivety, lacking responsibility
reason: The prompt opens with the words 'has limited awareness'. limited-awareness teaches it AND fixes the row's own failing — 'show it through a mistake or an assumption, never by telling us they are naive'. ordinary-world is a separate beat this archetype already has.
why: so we can measure how far they grow up by the end

label: Protagonist refuses again; stuck in ordinary world
reason: The beat is a SECOND refusal; ordinary-world teaches establishing normal life in Act 1. refusal teaches the move, including the action ('they go back, put it down, close the door').
why: so we see the flaw actively holding them back, not bad luck

label: The ordinary world
why: so the reader knows the life this story is about to break

label: We meet the protagonist in their lowly state
why: so the rise can be measured against exactly how low they started

label: Refuses the call; weakness revealed
why: so their weakness is on the page before they have to beat it

label: Protagonist decides to die with honour and glory
reason: self-sacrifice teaches surrender as 'the proof of the change' — but in tragedy dying for honour is the FLAW carried to the end, not growth. The concept would have a student write a redemptive scene into a tragedy.
why: so he goes down knowing the truth, choosing pride over survival

label: Protagonist willing to sacrifice for others
why: so the change is proved by what they are willing to lose

label: Dark Mentor dies
reason: Criterion 1 (mentor out of the way) fits, but criterion 2 — 'your protagonist then does the thing the mentor could not' — frames removal as triumph. A DARK mentor's death removes the last restraint and isolates him. Proposed: dark-mentor-falls — 'The Dark Mentor Falls'.
why: so he is left alone with the ruin his corrupter started

label: Dark Mentor fights the opposition and loses
reason: Same as above — the concept's heroic framing does not fit a corrupter being defeated in a tragedy.
why: so his last support is stripped before the end

label: Hero surpasses the Dark Mentor
reason: Shape fits, but the concept assumes a benign mentor and a heroic surpassing; in tragedy 'surpassing' means outdoing the corrupter in ruthlessness. Missing: a tragedy-side criterion.
why: so we see he has gone further into darkness than his corrupter did

label: Hero surpasses the Mentor
why: so the final win is theirs alone, not the mentor's

label: Mentor fights dark forces and loses
why: so nobody else can save them — the fight has to be theirs

label: Mentor fights monster and loses
why: so the monster is proved unbeatable by anyone but them

label: Mentor fights villain and loses
why: so the last helper is removed and they must finish it alone

label: Mentor sacrifices himself to save the protagonist
reason: Removal is covered, but a sacrifice's distinct job — leaving the hero a debt and grief to carry into the final fight — is not taught anywhere in the concept.
why: so the hero carries a debt into the final fight

label: Hero and companions set out across hostile terrain
why: so the journey physically begins and turning back stops being easy

label: Protagonist crosses the threshold into the special world
why: so the commitment is a physical act the reader can see

label: Small group of allies may welcome the protagonist
reason: Matched on the words 'into the special world' only. The beat is about WHO welcomes him; threshold teaches the physical crossing and gives no help designing the group.
why: so he is not alone when the change starts — someone lets him in

label: Small group of allies welcomes the Hero
reason: Same false match on 'into the special world'. Also note the archetype split: in tragedy this welcoming group flatters and enables rather than supports — a divergence that argues for a tragedy-specific row.
why: so the team we will follow is introduced as the new world opens

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so the crowd that flatters him into the special world seals his fall

label: Dark force accuses protagonist of being the same; not fooled
why: so he proves by acting that he is no longer what he was

label: Protagonist accuses opponents; opponent does not listen
reason: The roles are INVERTED: the protagonist accuses and is ignored, and it fails. The concept teaches the antagonist accusing and the hero answering with an action — a student would write the wrong scene entirely. Proposed: accusation-unheard — 'The Accusation Nobody Hears'.
why: so his last chance to be understood fails and the fall completes

label: Villain accuses protagonist of being the same; not fooled
why: so they must prove the difference by what they do next

label: Allies abandon the protagonist
why: so the tragic hero faces the end alone, with nobody left to stop them

label: Allies disagree on what to do next
why: so the protagonist is stripped of support right before the hardest part

label: Hero becomes separated from what's important
reason: Concept teaches a GROUP splitting; this beat is losing the person, place or thing that had become the anchor — if the student's 'important thing' is not an ally, the concept gives them nothing. Job also differs between the two archetypes.
why: so losing what mattered most forces them to prove who they really are

why_by_archetype.rags-to-riches: so what they gained is torn away and must be re-earned honestly
why_by_archetype.the-quest: so the goal costs them something they thought they could keep

label: Obstacles, crises with those once close to
reason: Concept teaches ONE split moment; the beat asks for SEVERAL escalating crises. Missing: escalation — each clash worse than the last (the 'obstacles' teaching) layered onto the relational break.
why: so the hero's fall costs them everyone who could have pulled them back

label: An ally betrays the protagonist
why: so the danger becomes personal and the protagonist can trust only themselves

label: FIRST EPIPHANY: moment of genuine insight
why: so the change starts small and the reader believes the later transformation

label: SECOND EPIPHANY: deeper realisation
reason: All three epiphanies share one concept, so it cannot ladder them. Missing here: this insight is about the SELF (not the world) and must change how they ACT — reactive to purposeful. The criteria still say 'a step, not the ending', which under-pitches it.
why: so the protagonist stops reacting and starts choosing what happens next

label: THIRD EPIPHANY: enlightened, possibly via redemption figure
reason: The concept's criterion 'they need not understand ALL of it yet' directly CONTRADICTS the beat ('they fully understand the truth they could not see when they set out'). The example (Scrooge asking about Tiny Tim) is a first-epiphany example. The 'redemption figure' delivering the truth is untaught.
why: so the reader sees the change is real, not just a scare

label: THIRD EPIPHANY: protagonist becomes enlightened
reason: Same contradiction as the other third epiphany — the concept tells the student to hold back full understanding when the beat requires it. Worse: this row spans tragedy, where the beat is the too-late recognition and the correct concept is tragic-acceptance ('sees the truth too late — and goes on anyway'), a genuinely different job.
why: so the hero finally understands the truth the whole journey was teaching

why_by_archetype.heros-journey: so the hero finally understands the truth the journey was always teaching
why_by_archetype.coming-of-age: so they finally understand what no adult could simply tell them
why_by_archetype.overcoming-the-monster: so they understand the monster well enough to actually beat it
why_by_archetype.rags-to-riches: so they learn the riches were never the thing that mattered
why_by_archetype.the-quest: so they see the goal was never what they set out for
why_by_archetype.voyage-and-return: so they carry home understanding, not just a story about somewhere strange
why_by_archetype.tragedy: so the hero sees the truth too late, and the loss means something

label: Allies pull out their own bag of tricks
reason: The concept insists 'your protagonist must be the one who does it' — the beat is the ALLIES acting. The student is told the opposite of what the beat asks. The real teaching is the pay-off of the distinct skill each ally was introduced with.
why: so every ally you introduced earns their place in the ending

label: Dark forces accuse protagonist of being the same; not fooled
reason: There is an exact concept already — villain-accuses ('You Are the Same as Me': the claim should be PARTLY TRUE, and the answer is an action not an argument). The regex branch 'final attempt' stole this row for fatal-blow, which teaches the decisive killing act instead.
why: so the protagonist proves the riches did not make them the villain

label: Hero emerges to win the prize
reason: Stage VI aftermath beat — CLAIMING the prize, not striking the blow. fatal-blow would have the student rewrite the previous beat. What is needed: the prize must be the thing set up at the start, and be shown being taken.
why: so the reader finally gets the payoff the whole story promised

label: Monster attacks the protagonist in final attempt
reason: The beat is the MONSTER attacking; the concept teaches the protagonist's own decisive act ('your protagonist must be the one who does it'). nightmare-battle is the right home — the external danger forcing the internal choice in one event.
why: so the monster is most dangerous exactly when the hero must win

label: Glimpse of true self; warmer humanity, potential to change
why: so the reader believes redemption is possible before it happens

label: Protagonist shows glimpse of true self
why: so the reader roots for them and believes they could succeed later

label: Has he/she changed or was it all just a dream?
why: so the ending proves the change instead of just claiming it

label: Has he/she grown or was it all just a dream?
why: so the reader can see exactly what the journey was worth

label: How much has the protagonist learnt?
why: so the story answers the question it asked at the start

label: But things begin to go wrong
why: so the reader sees the dream souring before the hero does

label: But things continue to go wrong
reason: 'Continue' means this is the second, deeper decline; mood-turns teaches a one-time shift in FEEL and tells the student to compare against an earlier scene they have already used. world-deteriorates ('measurably WORSE while your protagonist watches') carries the escalation this beat needs.
why: so the reader watches their world darken while they refuse to change

label: FRUSTRATION
why: so the easy way stops working and they must change approach

label: Hero begins to feel frustrated
why: so the hero's impatience pushes them towards the choice that destroys them

label: Mood changes to frustration, difficulty, or oppression
why: so the reader can measure how far things have fallen since the start

label: Hero becomes focused on this object
why: so the reader knows exactly what the hero will destroy themselves chasing

label: Some object of desire presents itself
why: so the hero has something to want that will cost them everything

label: Attacked again; resistance does not work
reason: The concept is literally 'The First Attack' and teaches 'the opposition touches them for the FIRST time' — this beat is explicitly 'attacked AGAIN'. The student is handed the wrong occasion. Also untaught: they lose because they cannot yet use the elixir they were given.
why: so losing twice proves they must change, not just try harder

label: Protagonist suffers a physical attack
why: so the reader learns the danger is real and the goal is not free

label: Protagonist returns with elixir; mastered himself
why: so the change is proved by what they give back, not what they say

label: Protagonist returns with elixir; newfound wisdom
why: so the community gains something from the journey, not just the hero

label: Protagonist returns with elixir; newfound wisdom and maturity
why: so growing up is shown by what they can now give others

label: Protagonist returns with the elixir; newfound wisdom
why: so the journey changes the world the hero left, not only the hero

label: A shadowy figure may appear
reason: The concept teaches total domination ('the opposition is now the STRONGEST thing in your story'); this beat is a single glimpse of something that 'may' appear. monster-distant's teaching — withhold the thing itself, the less you show the larger it feels — is exactly the help a portent needs.
why: so the reader feels the doom closing in before it arrives

label: Dark power begins to dominate
why: so the reader sees how much must be overcome for redemption to count

label: Monster begins to dominate; powerful forces unleashed
why: so beating the monster later actually means something

label: Shadow begins to dominate; powerful forces unleashed
why: so the opposition is strong enough to make the victory worth reading

label: Main character's flaw is revealed
why: so the story has something to fix, and the ending can prove it

label: Main character's flaw revealed (may be another character's flaw)
reason: The beat's distinctive rebirth mechanic — the flaw may belong to ANOTHER central character whom the protagonist must arc — is entirely untaught. The concept assumes the flaw is the protagonist's, so a student choosing the displaced version gets no help deciding whose flaw drives the story.
why: so we know exactly what must change before redemption can be believed

label: Time is running out to change
why: so the redemption has a deadline the reader can feel slipping away

label: Dark forces demonstrate their power again
why: so the new position is nearly taken back before they defend it

label: Dark power demonstrates its power again
why: so the pull back to the old self is at its strongest

label: Monster advances like a bulldozer
why: so the reader sees the monster is unstoppable unless the hero changes

label: Monster demonstrates his power again
why: so the final fight feels genuinely dangerous, not a formality

label: Opposition advances
why: so the walls close in while the hero keeps making things worse

label: Opposition demonstrates his power again
why: so the hero's fall is caused by a force stronger than them

label: Villain advances like a bulldozer
why: so the danger keeps growing while the protagonist is still not ready

label: Villain demonstrates his power again
why: so the reader doubts they can win right before they do

label: Goal becomes much more specific
reason: Beat sits in Stage III where the goal merely sharpens; the concept's 'last stretch is the worst / preparations before going in' half is a Stage V approach and misleads here.
why: so the reader knows exactly what winning would look like

label: Hero arrives within sight of goal
why: so the reader feels how close success is before the hardest part

label: Hero becomes committed to his course of action
reason: Beat is the point of no return, not sighting a goal; only the concept's 'what they decide or give up' line touches it. Threshold teaches the irreversible crossing this beat needs.
why: so the fall is his own choice, not bad luck

label: Hero makes preparations to defend winnings
reason: Swept in by the bare word 'preparations'. Approach teaches moving TOWARD a goal; this tragedy beat is protecting a prize already taken, where each act of protection is a fresh crime. Proposed: 'defending-the-prize' — Defending the Prize.
why: so keeping the prize costs him more than winning it did

label: Protagonist makes preparations for battle
why: so the reader sees what the fight will cost before it starts

label: Protagonist makes preparations to change
reason: Same 'preparations' regex sweep. There is no external goal in sight here — the preparation is internal and rebirth-only. 'A Way to Fix It' (a decision plus an action, first plan, too simple to work) is exactly this beat.
why: so the change looks earned, not a sudden switch at the end

label: Given supernatural or visionary direction; ONLY HE/SHE can solve it
reason: The generic Call is already covered by the 'INCITING INCIDENT' row in the same stage; what is distinctive here — a visionary/prophetic message and the chosen-one claim — is what Prophecy teaches (believed, incomplete or double-edged).
why: so the reader accepts that only this person can do it

label: Hero experiences a Call to confront it
why: so the hero must face the monster instead of hiding from it

label: INCITING INCIDENT - CALL TO ADVENTURE
why: so the old life ends and the story properly starts

label: Something calls or sends protagonist into wider world
why: so they leave the small world where they could never rise

label: Focused on solving a very simple problem
why: so the story starts small and believable, not with a grand mission

label: Protagonist's goal is a façade at this stage
why: so the real need can surface later and surprise them

label: If the protagonist's life stays the same, figurative death
why: so the reader knows what is lost if nothing changes

label: Protagonist sees life as oppressive, even though has a lot
reason: Beat is about restless appetite despite plenty — the discontent that feeds the tragic ambition. The concept asks the student to name a LOSS, which is not what this beat shows. False Balance ('looks steady from outside — show the crack') is the job here.
why: so his hunger for more looks inevitable before he does anything wrong

label: Protagonist's life is oppressive because he is alone
why: so his loneliness is the thing the redemption has to undo

label: Hero looks for unusual gratification
why: so we see the appetite that will destroy him before it does

label: Highlight the immaturity that needs to be overcome
why: so we can measure how far they have grown by the end

label: Protagonist has limited awareness, disconnected from reality
why: so his blindness explains the harm he does to other people

label: Protagonist has limited awareness, disconnected, unfulfilled
why: so his blindness, not bad luck, starts the fall

label: Protagonist has limited awareness, naive, ignorant...
why: so the reader can watch them learn what they do not know

label: New Information: second Catalyst, choice to continue
why: so going on is a deliberate choice, not just stubbornness

label: Greater obstacles before getting the prize
why: so the prize feels earned rather than handed over

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so each obstacle drags him deeper instead of teaching him

label: Obstacles and crises; more chances to change
reason: Escalation is only half the beat. The rebirth-specific half — repeated chances and reasons to change, which he keeps waving away — is taught by Warning Ignored, not by Rising Obstacles.
why: so refusing to change again makes the final change cost more

label: Protagonist encounters further monsters and temptations
why: so the middle keeps rising instead of drifting

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so every temptation taken makes the next crime easier

label: Protagonist experimenting and learning from tests
reason: Obstacles teaches escalation of difficulty; this beat is the hero LEARNING from tests, allies and enemies — acquiring the skill and knowledge that makes the later win credible. Nothing in the 70 covers it. Proposed: 'tests-and-learning' — Tests, Allies and Enemies.
why: so the hero earns the skills the final fight will demand

label: Hero feels terrible and disgusted with false identity

label: Protagonist starts to become more open to change
why: so the change later is not sudden — the door opens first

label: The hero seems powerless
why: so we feel the old self holding him down, not just hear it

label: The hero seems tiny and alone
reason: Overcoming-the-monster, Stage IV: nothing to do with a false identity or a mask. The beat is scale and isolation against a monster at its strongest — The Shadow Dominates ('show its reach; one image of the world under it') is the concept.
why: so the monster feels overwhelming and beating it means something

label: Things going downhill; trouble letting go of old self
why: so the reader believes how hard letting go really is

label: Protagonist comes back from dead; one last attempt to change
why: so the final change comes from something planted earlier, not luck

label: Protagonist comes back from dead; one last attempt to destroy monster
why: so the hero's return to fight is earned, not a lucky rescue

label: Protagonist comes back from the dead for one last attempt
why: so the last attempt is powered by something we already met

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so his last effort raises hope the ending will crush

label: Reversal: Mentor or ally brings protagonist back to life
why: so the rescue pays off someone the reader already knows

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so the brief hope makes the coming destruction hurt more

label: Hero excited or fascinated by the new world
why: so the thrill of the new life hides the danger inside it

label: Hero is excited or fascinated by the new world
why: so the reader feels the wonder before the world turns on them

label: Protagonist excited or fascinated by the new world
why: so the escape feels exciting before it starts costing him

label: Protagonist is presented with a sword
why: so the new identity has an object the reader can see

label: Protagonist receives apparent wisdom and ambiguous gifts
reason: The word 'apparent' and 'ambiguous' is the whole beat — a tragedy gift that is double-edged and misleads him. The Gift teaches an object that MEANS the change; it says nothing about a promise that comes true in a way he never meant. Prophecy teaches exactly that.
why: so his confidence rests on advice that was never what it seemed

label: Protagonist receives crucial wisdom and/or gifts
why: so they enter the final test holding something they lacked before

label: Protagonist receives new clothes, symbolic of new identity
why: so the change is visible on the outside, not just stated

why_by_archetype.tragedy: so the new role never quite fits the man wearing it

label: Forces of opposition and fate closing in
reason: Tragic Acceptance is about recognition — seeing the truth too late and going on. This beat is external pressure tightening, before any recognition. Cornered ('close every exit; name the cost of losing') is the job.
why: so escape is impossible and the ending feels inevitable

label: Protagonist accepts his/her fate forever
why: so he faces the ending he made instead of being rescued

label: Protagonist reflects on past mistakes; expresses regret
why: so the reader sees him understand, exactly when it is too late

label: Opponent understands the protagonist's weakness
reason: The mapping is the beat REVERSED — the concept teaches the protagonist working out the ANTAGONIST's flaw, while this tragedy beat is the opponent working out the PROTAGONIST's. The Lion King example coaches the opposite move. Proposed: 'flaw-exploited' — The Flaw Turned Against Them (fallback: the-flaw).
why: so he is destroyed by his own flaw, not by chance

label: Protagonist understands the dark force's weakness
why: so the dark force is beaten by understanding, not by luck

label: Protagonist understands the dark forces' weakness
why: so the underdog wins by working it out, not by luck

label: Protagonist understands the monster's weakness
why: so the monster is beaten by cleverness the reader can follow

label: Protagonist understands the villain's weakness
why: so the win comes from something the hero noticed earlier

label: B Story: discussion about the Theme
why: so the story's truth gets said out loud by people, not the author

label: Dark forces appear to have cornered the protagonist
why: so the reader stops seeing a way out, and fears they lose everything

label: Hero may fall into the monster's clutches
why: so the monster feels genuinely deadly before the hero can beat it

label: Hero may fall into the shadow's clutches
why: so the reader believes the hero could actually lose here

why: so the collapse feels earned — one failure knocking over the next

label: Greater crises
why: so the danger keeps rising instead of repeating, and the reader stays hooked

label: Compelled to commit dark acts
reason: lowest-point teaches despair and being stripped bare; this beat is the protagonist ACTING — committing worse deeds to protect the first one. The branch 'compelled to commit dark acts' was bolted onto the regex.
why: so each crime forces the next, and turning back stops being possible

label: Compelled to run away from the truth
reason: missing how to write avoidance: lowest-point teaches the bottom (goal lost, ally stripped), but this beat is a second refusal — refusal teaches saying no because of the flaw, with an action.
why: so he is given one last chance to face it, and refuses

label: Lowest point; mounting sense of threat and despair
reason: in tragedy the third criterion is false — it promises 'the change has to be EARNED out of this, later', but a tragic protagonist does not come back up; the tragedy-specific note is missing.
why: so the bottom is real, and nothing after it can rescue him

label: Suddenly realises things will never be the same
reason: this is a RECOGNITION beat, not a despair beat; lowest-point's 'strip the ally, mask goes back on' does not teach how to write a realisation landing on a character.
why: so he finally sees there is no going back to who he was

label: This is his/her lowest point
why: so the change afterwards has to be earned, not simply handed over

label: Dark forces are dealt a fatal blow
reason: nick-of-time teaches only the TIMING; the beat's job is the decisive act itself, and fatal-blow ('your protagonist must be the one who does it') is the lesson this beat needs — its regex already contains 'fatal blow' but nick-of-time claims the row first.
why: so the thing that oppressed them is beaten, by them, on the page

label: Dark forces dealt a fatal blow; goal is won
reason: same over-claim: fatal-blow's regex matches both 'fatal blow' and 'goal is won', and it teaches the decisive act; nick-of-time teaches only pace.
why: so the quest is finished by the hero's own hand, not by luck

label: In the nick of time, the protagonist changes
reason: the beat is the REDEMPTION TURN, not an escape; nick-of-time teaches escape timing and short sentences, which gives a rebirth student nothing. seizes-sword teaches the mask coming off visibly.
why: so the change comes late enough to cost him and still save him

label: In the nick of time, the protagonist escapes
why: so the escape is won by seconds, and the danger stays believable

label: Monster is dealt a fatal blow
reason: the beat is the kill, not the clock; fatal-blow teaches that the protagonist must land it on the page rather than have it summarised.
why: so the monster dies by the hero's hand, in a scene we watch

label: More obstacles, crises and conflicts; thrilling escape
reason: this sits at STAGE III (escalation), not the finale — nick-of-time claimed it on the words 'thrilling escape'. The beat's job is rising obstacles, which is exactly what the obstacles concept teaches.
why: so the danger grows step by step before the real fight arrives

label: Obstacles, betrayal, crises and conflicts
reason: STAGE III escalation beat mis-claimed by 'thrilling escape'; obstacles teaches escalation, and the betrayal clause is served by the betrayal concept, not by escape timing.
why: so each setback is harder, and growing up costs something real

label: Obstacles, crises and conflicts ending in thrilling escape
reason: same STAGE III mis-claim: the row is about mounting obstacles, and nick-of-time only teaches the last-second win.
why: so the journey gets harder each time, and progress feels earned

label: Protagonist struggles to escape
reason: archetype-blind mis-claim, and it teaches the OPPOSITE of the beat: nick-of-time promises the win 'lands with nothing to spare', but this is tragedy — the struggle must fail. A tragedy student is being told to write a rescue.
why: so we watch him fight, and still lose — the loss must be earned

label: Final Image: opposite of Opening Image
reason: the /opening image/i regex claims the row because the label contains the words; the final-image concept exists and teaches exactly this beat (mirror the opening, changed, show don't explain).
why: so the reader SEES the change instead of being told about it

label: Opening Image represents the central struggle & tone
why: so the first picture already carries the story's struggle and its mood

label: Snapshot of the main character's problem
why: so we watch the problem happen instead of being told about it

label: Protagonist sees a way to fix it
why: so the story has a plan simple enough to go wrong later

why: so dread builds before anything happens, and the reader feels it coming

label: A storm is coming; onset of evil felt in the air
why: so the air changes before the danger does, and tension starts early

label: A storm is coming; something threatening
why: so the reader senses the ruin coming while the hero does not

why: so we understand why he became this, before we watch him change

label: Painful past experience revealed
why: so the flaw has a cause, and changing later feels possible
